thread.title: Are volatile stocks a black swan moment after another big drop for Dow?

author: Mike Sunnucks
title: Are volatile stocks a black swan moment after another big drop for Dow?
text: – Senior Reporter, Phoenix  20pm MST Market downturns and the end of expansion cycles (i.e. recessions) don’t start with a whimper. They usually land with a resounding thud. That is according Spencer Levy . He’s head of research for commercial real estate firm CBRE Group Inc. (NYSE: CBG). He was in Phoenix Thursday to talk about the state of real estate markets and the economy. It also just happens to the be the second day this week the Dow Jones Industrial Average closed down more than 1,000 points following Monday’s big 1,100-point loss. Levy said the test of the economy — including consumers, business sentiment and real estate markets — is whether the stress with stocks turns into a “black swan” event that upsets the current and long economic expansion. Economists point to black swans as unexpected events that upset markets, consumers and businesses and turn the tables on the overall economy. The 30-stock Dow lost 4.15 percent today, the S&P 500 was down 3.75 percent while the VIX Volatility Index was up 24 percent ending at 34.53. The VIX was in the 10- to 15-point range last year during stocks' record bull run. Yields for 10- and 30-year U.S. Treasury notes were also up today again. Higher yields for Treasuries and bonds along with a high VIX pushes down on stocks. Levy said markets and investors likely had “a false sense of security” with the VIX’s low levels last year. Now, the CBRE research head says the stock market volatility is testing more than investors and Wall Street. He is waiting to see if it has impacts on consumer spending and confidence. “It’s more damaging psychologically,” said Levy in an interview with the Business Journal. The current expansion started in 2009 though markets hit hard by the last real estate induced crash such as Phoenix and Las Vegas came out of the downturn later. The flip side is that other parts of the economy — Christmas retail sales, job gains, wage and expected GDP growth and real estate — have been performing well. Apple Inc . (Nasdaq: AAPL) announced a $350 billion U.S. investment effort after tax cuts passed by Congress and President Donald Trump . Amazon.com (Nasdaq: AMZN) is landing a second $5 billion headquarters in one of 20 U.S. cities. And even retailers battling Amazon and e-commerce such as Kohl’s (NYSE: KSS) and Macy’s (NYSE: M) reported better than expected holiday same-store sales. Wages grew by 2.9 percent last year, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. And a number of companies including Starbucks (Nasdaq: SBUX), American Airlines (Nasdaq: AAL) and Wells Fargo (NYSE: WFC) have given bonuses from their windfalls from the Trump tax cuts. Levy said other potential black swans for the economy such as a trade war or international conflict aren't on the horizon. But stock market induced stress could move beyond Wall Street, mutual funds and 401(k) accounts. – Senior Reporter, Phoenix  20pm MST
